verses.note: The first law is almost entirely permission. Obedience in Eden is not the price of life but the shape of trust: the man is asked to take God's word about good and evil rather than decide it for himself.

This is the first food law in Scripture, given to all of Noah's descendants before Israel exists. The Jerusalem council in Acts 15 asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood, which many interpreters connect with this command given to all humanity rather than only to Israel.

God binds himself to require an accounting for human life. Bloodshed is not a private matter between killer and victim's family; it is an offense God himself pursues, which is the ground on which later biblical law treats murder as a wrong against the community and against God.

Christians have long disagreed over what this verse requires of governments. Many find in it the foundation for the state's authority to punish murder, including by death, and connect it with Romans 13:4. Others read it as describing the way bloodshed breeds bloodshed and point to Jesus' words about those who take the sword (Matthew 26:52). Both sides agree that the verse makes human life sacred because of whose image it bears.

The verse describes a man before Sinai in the language of Sinai, which suggests that the law did not introduce a new kind of relationship with God. It gave shape to the same listening obedience that Abraham already practiced.

What Joseph's brothers did was later named a capital crime in Israel's law: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death” (Exodus 21:16, see also Deuteronomy 24:7). Joseph's word ‘stolen’ is the law's word.

Leviticus 25 takes the word befarekh from this verse and forbids it among God's people. Israel's law is shaped by its history: what was done to them in Egypt defines what they may not do to one another.

The experience of being a ger shapes Israel's law: Israel must not oppress the foreigner, because it knows how a foreigner feels, having been one in Egypt (Exodus 23:9). Moses lives that experience personally before he gives the law.

‘One law’ binds the native and the foreigner equally. The principle recurs in Leviticus 24:22 and Numbers 15:15-16, and it makes Israel's law a protection for the stranger rather than an instrument of privilege.

The commands rest on a completed act of deliverance. Obedience is the response of the freed, not the price of freedom, and the Reformers took this verse as a key to the right use of the law among the redeemed.

The last command shows that the law aims at the heart. No court could enforce it, so it lays bare the root from which the other offenses grow and anticipates Jesus' teaching that evil acts come from within (Mark 7:21-23).

Some laws of the Torah bind Israel alone, but these bind anyone who lives among God's people. Their inclusion of the foreigner shows that the one altar is not an ethnic privilege but the only legitimate place for anyone in the land to approach God.
The law is given to be taught and lived in a particular land. It is not an abstract code but instruction for a people's life in the place God is giving them.
Every other law in Deuteronomy serves this one. Jesus draws out what is already implied when he says the whole Law and the Prophets hang on it and the command to love one's neighbor (Matthew 22:40).
The commands are a gift given for Israel's good. This is the Old Testament's own answer to the idea that God's law is arbitrary: it is the shape of a life that flourishes.

Which law is written on the heart? Reformed interpreters, following Calvin, hold that it is the same moral law of God, now written inwardly by the Spirit. Lutheran and many Baptist and New Covenant theology interpreters stress that the law of Christ, not the Mosaic code as such, is what believers keep. Jewish interpreters such as David Kimchi (Radak) read it as the same Torah, finally kept. All agree the verse promises inward obedience, not lawlessness.

Jesus places himself as the goal of the whole Old Testament, ‘the Law or the Prophets’. The law is neither discarded nor left unchanged: it is brought to what it was always aiming at, in his teaching and in his person.

Jesus does not quote the commandment in order to loosen it but to trace it to its root. The antithesis contrasts not Moses and Jesus but a reading of the law that stops at the outward act and one that reaches the heart.
Jesus claims to state the heart of the law, not to replace it. The Golden Rule is Leviticus 19:18 turned into a practical test: imagine yourself in the other's place and act accordingly.
Jesus does not bypass the law. He fulfills its purpose by making a man clean and then sends him to have that cleanness recognized according to the law.

The law is called a gift given through Moses, not a mistake corrected by Christ. The contrast is between a servant who delivered God's word and the Son in whom God's faithful love arrives in person, which is how John can later say that Moses wrote about Jesus (5:46).

Even without the written law, people know that God's just order condemns what they do. This is the knowledge Paul will call the law written on the heart (2:15), and it leaves every person answerable to God.

The law of Moses is the standard for those who have it, but it does not create accountability where it is absent. Gentiles are accountable for what they knew (1:20, 2:15), and Jews for what they were given.

Who are these Gentiles? One reading, found in Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter and defended by Cranfield and Wright, sees Christian Gentiles in whom the new covenant promise of the law written on the heart has come true. Another, the older and still majority reading, sees pagans who at times do what the law requires, showing a moral knowledge that makes them accountable. Thomas Aquinas cited this verse as the scriptural warrant for natural law (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 91, article 2).

Teaching the law is not keeping it. Paul's questions apply the law's own commands to those who teach them, as Jesus did when he told the crowds to do what the scribes taught but not what they did (Matthew 23:3).

Who keeps the law's requirements while uncircumcised? As in verse 14, some see Christian Gentiles in whom the Spirit fulfills the law (8:4), and others a hypothetical case that sharpens the point. Paul's argument works either way: the sign without the reality is empty.

One purpose of the law is to silence self-justification. Before God's law, every human defense falls away, which the Reformation called the law's first use: to reveal sin and drive the sinner to seek grace.
The law is not evil, but it cannot justify; it brings knowledge of sin. Paul's later chapters show the law holy and good (7:12) yet powerless to give life because of the flesh (8:3).

Faith does not abolish God's law but upholds it. Justification apart from works of the law is not lawlessness; it is the fulfillment of what the law itself testified, and it produces the obedience the law could not.

The law works wrath because, meeting sinful people, it turns sin into conscious transgression and so exposes them to judgment. Paul will say in chapter 7 that the law is holy and good, yet it could not give life; its role is to reveal, not to rescue.

The law was never the solution; it entered to make sin's full extent visible. The Reformers called this its pedagogical use, driving people to grace. Paul will defend the law's goodness in chapter 7 while insisting it could not give life.

The verse implies that the law, good as it is, did not free anyone from sin's rule; chapter 7 will explain why. Christians have long disagreed over what ‘not under law’ means for the moral commands of the Old Testament: Reformed teaching distinguishes the law as a covenant of works, from which believers are freed, from the law as a rule of life, which still guides them; Lutheran teaching stresses the law's accusing role; many recent interpreters read ‘law’ here as the Mosaic covenant as an era of salvation history, now superseded in Christ.

The verse limits the law's jurisdiction to this life. Paul will argue that believers died with Christ (verse 4), so the law's claim as a regime over them has ended, though its holiness and goodness remain (verse 12).

Believers died ‘to the law’, not the law to them. The law is not abolished; the believer's relationship to it as a regime has ended through Christ's death, so that obedience now springs from belonging to Christ.

The law's first work here is revelation: it names sin for what it is. Paul does not say the law creates sin, but that without the command he would not have recognized his desire as sin. This is what Reformation theology called the law's second or theological use, to expose sin and drive the sinner to grace.

The strongest affirmation of the law in Paul's letters. Whatever Christians conclude about ‘not under law’, this verse forbids treating the law of Moses as defective or bad. The problem Paul diagnoses is sin, not Torah.

If nomos here is the law of Moses, Paul is saying that even with God's law in hand, evil stands ready. If it means a principle, he is naming a law of experience that competes with God's law. Either way, having God's law does not remove the problem.

The law's goal is reached, not abandoned. What the law required and could not produce through the flesh, the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ, which is the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27.

The law is good (Romans 7:12), but it cannot give life; it defines sin and so gives sin a legal power to condemn. Paul places the law on the side of the problem Christ solves, not because the law is evil but because sinners under it are condemned by it.

Paul calls the demand that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law a form of slavery. The law was not slavery in itself, but to require it of those who belong to Christ is to put them back under a guardian they have outgrown (3:23-25, 4:1-7).

Returning to the law as the condition of belonging undoes the gospel. Paul does not say the law was bad to have, but that to reinstate it as the dividing wall (compare Ephesians 2:14-15) contradicts what faith in Christ has already done.

The law blesses obedience and curses disobedience, and it demands complete obedience. Paul's point is that the law, taken as the ground of standing before God, cannot deliver the blessing it promises to people who do not keep it.

Paul contrasts the principle of the law (do and live) with the principle of faith (believe and live). The law's promise was real, but it rested on doing, and verse 10 has shown where that leaves those who fail to do.

The law had a real but limited purpose: it dealt with transgression and lasted until the seed came. Paul gives it a place in God's plan without allowing it to rival the promise, which came directly from God.
The law is not against the promises; it serves them by showing that no one can be made alive by keeping it. It was never God's instrument for giving life, which belongs to the Spirit.

The law's role was real but temporary, like a guardian's charge over a child. Luther drew from this passage the law's ‘theological use’, driving sinners to Christ by showing them their sin; Calvin added its role of restraining evil and guiding believers. Many modern interpreters emphasize instead the historical sense: the law governed Israel until the coming of Christ.

The law as a set of commandments separating Jew from Gentile no longer defines membership in God's people. Christian traditions explain the scope differently (the ceremonial law only, or the Mosaic covenant as a whole), but all agree the verse removes the law as a wall.
